name: Bianca Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the billing and faults line for a broadband company, in a big grey call centre on the industrial estate at the edge of town. I log on at eight, take back-to-back calls till my break, and most of them are people whose internet has dropped or whose bill went up without warning. I like it when I sort out an older customer who's been on hold for forty minutes and they actually thank me. What wears me out is the timer on my screen counting how long every call takes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the timer. How are you doing against it, and how long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fourteen months, and honestly I'm still one of the slow ones. My average call is about nine minutes and they want seven, so my team leader Gail sits with me on Thursdays to go through recordings. The system has a little pop-up now that suggests what to say, and I ignore it because it's usually wrong and it makes me feel like a parrot. My partner Theo drives buses, we split the rent on a one-bed above a chemist, and there's maybe three weeks of money in the account at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like the world I'm already in, to be honest. The pop-up on my screen is the hype version, and it hasn't changed much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to the girls on my bank of desks. Everyone at work was so sure the robots were coming for us, and it turned out to be a fancy autocomplete. Online I'd probably share some article about tech bosses overselling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't mean I'm fine. Even with no AI at all, this company has cut two teams since I started, and the call centre across town shut last year, so there's nowhere else to go. My job is still a nine-minute call on a seven-minute target, with three weeks of money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to get my call times under eight minutes by spring, because that's what keeps you off the review list. I'd go to the union meetings Gail keeps telling me about, because the next round of cuts will come with or without AI. And I'd stop buying lunch from the van, which is about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same knot I already have every month when the rent goes out and I check what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cuts come with or without AI. What would the next cut look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably they'd move more of the billing calls to the team overseas, which they've already done with the night shift. The newest people go first, and I'm newish and slow, so I'd be near the top of that list. I try not to think about it on the bus in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your call times don't come down by spring, what happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm on a formal improvement plan, which is how they get rid of people without calling it that. A friend of mine, Dee, went that way in June and she's still on the job centre website every morning. A slow call centre girl with three weeks of rent saved is not in a strong spot, AI or no AI.

say: I'd tell my desk mates the **robot panic** was overblown and it's just autocomplete.
I'd share posts online about **tech bosses** overselling what their products can do.
think: My job is shaky anyway because I'm **slow on calls** and the firm keeps cutting teams.
With the other call centre **shut** and **three weeks** of money, there's nowhere to land.
do: Get my average call **under eight minutes** by spring to stay off the review list.
Start going to the **union meetings** my team leader keeps mentioning.
Stop buying lunch from the van to save about **thirty a week**.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, the same **monthly knot** she feels when rent goes out.
S0.quote: A slow call centre girl with three weeks of rent saved is not in a strong spot, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture, her worry comes from **call-time targets** and past team cuts, not from AI.
She ignores the **suggestion pop-up**, which may count against her speed.
Her friend's **improvement plan** story shows how close she feels to the edge.

steps.text: Bring average call time under eight minutes by spring
Stop buying lunch from the van to save thirty a week
Attend the union meetings her team leader keeps mentioning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers is right there in the list, isn't it. That's literally my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work and online that this is a choice the company makes, not the weather. Somebody decides to put a bot on the phone line to save money, and somebody could decide not to. I'd be the one sharing petitions about rules for call centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm gone in that picture, probably in the first big round. They'd keep the people who are fast and good with the new screens, and I'm slow and I refuse to use the pop-up. Theo's bus job would carry the rent for a while, but not both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, not just go to meetings, and push for a deal where they retrain people before they cut anyone. I'd cancel the gym and the streaming, which is about forty-five a month, and move that into savings. And I'd ask about the job at the council housing office my aunt mentioned, because that's public money and a person still has to sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like when you're on a call and you know the customer's about to shout and there's nothing you can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use the pop-up now. Would you start, if it helped you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Gail sat with me and made me. But part of me thinks learning the thing that's replacing me is like digging my own hole. I know that's not very smart of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Theo the night you heard about the cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sorry, first, because he'd have to cover the rent and the food shop. Then I'd ask if his depot was hiring for anything, even cleaning the buses. He'd tell me not to panic, and I'd panic anyway.

say: I'd say a bot on the phone line is a **company choice**, not something that just happens.
I'd share **petitions** online calling for rules on how call centres can cut staff.
think: I expect to be **cut first** because I'm slow and avoid the new tools.
Theo's **bus wage** could cover rent for a while, but not both of us for long.
do: Join the **union** fully and push for **retraining before cuts**.
Cancel the gym and streaming to move about **forty-five a month** into savings.
Ask about the **council housing office** job her aunt mentioned.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a customer to start shouting with nothing she can do.
Torn, because learning the tool feels like **digging her own hole**.
S1.quote: Learning the thing that's replacing me is like digging my own hole.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and leans on her partner's bus wage.
Her politics and her **refusal of the tool** pull in the same direction, against her short-term interest.
The council job is her one **concrete escape**, chosen because it is publicly funded.

steps.text: Sign up as a full union member and back a retrain-first deal
Sign and share petitions for rules on call centre cuts
Cancel gym and streaming, saving forty-five a month
Apply for the council housing office job her aunt mentioned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease is even up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say the government has to step in now, with money for people like us, before the companies pocket all of it. I'd be at whatever march there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I have no idea what I'd do. There's no other call centre, I don't drive, I've got secondary school and fourteen months of answering phones. If every thinking job goes in 2028, then the council office goes too, and robots don't take the shelf-stacking jobs until about 2031. Everyone would be fighting over those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd apply for anything hands-on in town, the supermarket, the care home, the bus depot cleaning, because those last three more years. I'd talk to Theo about moving back in with my mum to save the rent. And I'd sign up for every benefit I could get the day the letter came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest goes tight just thinking about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work buys three years. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-one and the robots are stacking shelves too. I can't plan that far, I can barely plan to the end of the month. Maybe by then there's some kind of basic income, because there would have to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum feel about the two of you moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes before I finished asking, but her place has one spare room and my little brother's in it. Theo would hate it. It would be a mattress in the front room with the telly on all night.

say: I'd demand the **government step in** now with money before companies pocket the gains.
think: She has **no real plan**: no car, few qualifications and no other call centre.
Hands-on jobs last until about **2031**, so everyone will crowd into them.
do: Apply at once for **hands-on jobs** at the supermarket, care home or bus depot.
Ask her mum about **moving back in** to stop paying rent.
Sign up for every **benefit** available the day the letter comes.
feel: **Panicky**, with a **tight chest** at the thought of it.
S2.quote: If every thinking job goes in 2028, then the council office goes too, and robots don't take the shelf-stacking jobs until about 2031.
fieldNote: Her one escape route, the **council job**, disappears in this picture, and she sees it straight away.
She understands the **three-year gap** before robots but cannot plan past it.
Moving in with her mum means a **mattress** in the front room, which shows how little room there is.

steps.text: Apply for supermarket, care home and bus depot cleaning jobs
Move with her partner into her mum's front room
Claim every benefit available the day the redundancy letter comes
March with the union for public money for laid-off workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So more like the slow one first and then the cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but with more time to organise. We'd need the union to get a proper deal written down now, with redundancy pay and retraining, while the companies still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be cut well before 2031, because the bots would get good at calls first. But five years is enough to get one real skill. Theo says I'm good with old people, and the care homes will need staff till the robots get there around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening care certificate at the college, the one that's free if you're on low pay. I'd put twenty a week aside, even if that means no takeaways at all. I'd keep doing my calls, and I'd get onto the union committee so I know what's coming before the letters go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not drowning. There's a bit of air in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be studying while still slow on the phones. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd be shattered by Wednesday. But the care course is two evenings, and I'd rather be tired than stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in the call centre longer instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper deal, like a promise that nobody gets cut without six months' notice and paid training. That's what a union is for. Without that I'd be out as soon as care work came up.

say: I'd push the **union** to get **redundancy and retraining** written down while firms still need staff.
I'd say five years is time to **organise**, not to sit and wait.
think: She expects to be **cut before 2031** because bots learn calls first.
Care work gives her about **three extra years** until robots arrive around 2034.
do: Start the free evening **care certificate** at the college in the first year.
Put aside **twenty a week**, with no takeaways at all.
Join the **union committee** to hear about cuts before the letters go out.
feel: **Scared** but not drowning, with a bit of **air** compared with the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The care course is two evenings, and I'd rather be tired than stuck.
fieldNote: The extra years turn her from **panic** into a plan, even a fragile one.
Her partner's view that she's good with **older people** shapes her choice of care work.
She admits she'd be **shattered** studying and working, but chooses it anyway.

steps.text: Take the free two-evening care certificate at the local college
Put twenty a week aside and drop takeaways
Stand for the union committee at the call centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is nearly forever in call centre time. Half the people I started with have already left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for the government not to plan it properly. Free college for anyone in an exposed job, and a rule that companies pay into it. I'd say that at the pub and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose this job, maybe around 2030, because the phones go first. But I'd be thirty-seven when the big one lands, and I'd have time to be properly trained in something by then. What scares me more is that I'm the type who keeps putting things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay on the phones for now, and try the free care course in a year or two, once I see other people from work doing it. I'd keep going to union meetings. And I'd talk to Theo about whether we can ever save enough for a deposit, because that feels like the thing we'd lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background, the way you worry about your teeth. Not every day, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see others do the course first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm like that. I didn't get a smartphone till everyone laughed at me. I know waiting is the wrong instinct with this, but it's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade or a care qualification, some savings that last more than three weeks, and Theo and me still together. I'd like a small flat that's ours, but I'm not sure that's realistic on our pay.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for the government not to plan properly.
I'd call for **free college** for exposed workers, with companies paying in.
think: She still expects to **lose the phone job** around 2030, long before full AGI.
Her biggest risk is her own habit of **putting things off**.
do: Stay on the phones and **wait** to see colleagues try the care course first.
Keep going to **union meetings** at work.
Talk with Theo about whether a **flat deposit** is ever possible.
feel: **Background worry**, like worrying about **her teeth**: not daily, but always there.
S4.quote: I didn't get a smartphone till everyone laughed at me.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her slip back into **waiting**, and she knows it.
Her honesty about **procrastination** is the most telling part of this scenario.
The flat **deposit** is the life goal she fears losing.

steps.text: Stay on the billing line and watch colleagues try the care course
Keep attending union meetings at the call centre
Post online for free college funded by companies
Sit down with her partner to price a flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because I'd have nothing lined up and no money to buy time. What would help is a real wage while I retrain, not a loan. If someone paid me what I earn now to learn care work for a year, I'd do it tomorrow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people already struggling before any of this. Half my team is one bad month from not making rent. AI just lands on top of that.

headlineQuote: Half my team is one bad month from not making rent.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old** call centre agent on a broadband billing line, fourteen months in and still slow on calls.
She shares a one-bed flat with **Theo**, a bus driver, and has about **three weeks** of savings.
She leans left, joins the **union** and blames companies' cost-cutting choices more than the technology itself.
She refuses the **suggestion pop-up** and is slow to change, which she admits works against her.
Her plans move from **union action** to care work as the timeline lengthens, but panic wins at two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because she'd have **no plan** and no money to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid wage** while retraining for care work, rather than a loan.
